fields.meta_title: Membership Survey With Renewal Follow-Up | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a membership survey that ranks benefits by use, flags low renewal scores to staff, and asks lapsed members why. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Membership Survey That Shows Why Members Renew
fields.hero_description: Build a membership survey that ties each answer to the member's tier and renewal date, with every response in your own database.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into the Survey
fields.features_subheading: Name your member types and benefits in one prompt. Emergent builds each part below, and a second prompt changes any of it.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that follow the member type

Emergent writes questions for each member type you name and adds the logic between them. A retired member skips the career questions, and a student sees the ones on student dues.
fields.feature_2:
Every answer tied to a member record

Upload your member list or connect your membership software by API. Every response carries the member's tier, join year, and renewal date. Any chart can split on those three.
fields.feature_3:
Benefits ranked by use and by value

The dashboard lists every benefit with how many members used it last year and how many rated it worth the dues. The board sees which benefits get used before it sets the next budget.
fields.feature_4:
Alerts when an answer needs a person

Set a rule on any question, such as a low renewal score or a billing complaint. The app emails the staff member who looks after that member, or posts in Slack, with the comment.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen on a phone

Members open the link from an email and answer one question at a time on their phone. A 12-question membership survey reads as 12 short screens instead of one long scrolling form.
fields.feature_6:
The survey's full code in your GitHub

On paid plans, Emergent exports the survey's full code, dashboard included, to your GitHub repository. Any developer can then review and extend it like any other code project.

fields.tab_content_1:
The print journal finishes last of five benefits

The Tamsworth Dental Hygienists' Association sends its 1,240 members a 15-question survey and keeps it open 10 days. Of the 434 who answer, 351 took a CE course last year and 83 read the print journal.
fields.tab_content_2:
A renewal score of 6 or lower goes to the club manager

Fernvault Fitness asks each member 30 days before renewal: how likely are you to renew, scored out of 10. At the Eastside club, 5 members answer this week and 2 score 6 or lower. Their plans and comments go by email to Paloma Arguello, the club manager. The other 3 score 7 or higher and get no follow-up.
fields.tab_content_3:
Cost of dues tops the reasons lapsed members give

Stoneflax Makerspace emails a 5-question survey to each member 14 days after their membership lapses. Of the 85 lapsed members who answer, 32 name the cost of dues and 23 say they stopped using the shop. Their comments go to Wren Castellanos, the membership lead, sorted by reason.
fields.tab_content_4:
Weekend visits split the Family tier from the rest

Wendmoor Science Museum members answer an 8-question survey on their phones, and each answer carries the member's tier. Only 37 of 118 Family members are satisfied with weekend visits, the lowest of any tier. Their comments point to crowded Saturdays.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Membership Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a membership survey members finish, then act on its answers before renewals come due.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the answers will change
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Export and clean your member list
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write questions that ask one thing
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the decisions this survey feeds: next year's dues, which benefits to keep, the event calendar. Cut any question that cannot change one of them. A survey built around three decisions stays short enough for members to finish.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Export name, email, tier, join date, and renewal date from your membership records, then clean the list. Merge duplicate records, fix emails that bounced, and leave lapsed members out of this send. A messy list skews the response rate before anyone answers.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask one thing per question and use the same 1-5 scale for every rating. Put the questions every member answers first and the tier-specific ones after. Keep the survey to 15 questions or fewer, and time yourself taking it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Paste the questions into a prompt with your tiers and any rule you want, such as who hears about a low renewal score. Emergent builds the survey, its database, and a results dashboard from that prompt, ready for a test run.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Test it as three different members
fields.howto_step_5_des: Open the survey as a student, a full member, and a retired member. Check that each sees the right questions, that answers land on the right member record, and that a low renewal score sends the alert you set.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Send it with a reason, remind once
fields.howto_step_6_des: Email the link with one line on what the board will decide with the answers. A week later, send one reminder to members who have not answered yet. Close the survey on the date you announced in the first email.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Report the results back to members
fields.howto_step_7_des: Within a month of closing, send members the top three findings and the change each one brings. Name one change already made, and link the full results for any member who wants the detail behind them.

faq_plan.q: What are some good questions to ask in a membership survey?
faq_plan.ref: What are some good questions to ask in a membership survey?

prov.original: What are some good questions to ask in a membership survey?

faq_plan.a: Good membership survey questions cover why the member joined, which benefits they used in the past year, and whether the dues feel fair for what they get. Add one question on how likely they are to renew and one on which emails they read. Close with an open question: what one change would make membership worth more?

faq_plan.q: How do I create a membership survey?
faq_plan.a: Create it by describing it. Write down the questions and who should hear about which answers, then give both to Emergent's AI survey builder. It builds the survey and its response database, and another prompt changes either one. Before the full send, pilot it with ten members from different tiers and fix whatever confuses them.

faq_plan.q: What should a member satisfaction survey measure?
faq_plan.a: A member satisfaction survey should measure how members rate what they already get, such as events and the value of their dues. Ask the same core questions every year to compare each score with last year's. Membership surveys can also ask why people joined or what they want next; keep those apart from the yearly set.

faq_plan.q: What does a membership survey template get wrong?
faq_plan.a: Its benefit list. A membership survey template is written around someone else's benefits, and a dental association's list does not fit a gym or a museum. A volunteer survey, for example, asks about shifts, training, and recognition instead of dues. List your own benefits first, then borrow the template's phrasing for each question.

faq_plan.q: What are some membership survey examples?
faq_plan.a: Four membership survey examples are worth running: a yearly needs survey, a renewal check, a survey for lapsed members, and a 90-day check-in for new members. The 90-day version asks whether membership matched what the new member expected. Emergent builds each one from a prompt, all on the same member database.

faq_plan.q: What should a gym member survey ask?
faq_plan.a: A gym member survey should ask about what members notice on every visit: crowding at peak hours, equipment that is broken or always taken, cleanliness, class times, and staff. Ask what time of day each member trains to tie crowding complaints to real hours. Send a shorter version to new members after their first month as well.

faq_plan.q: When is the best time to send a membership survey?
faq_plan.a: Send the yearly survey at a quiet point in your calendar, at least two months before the board sets next year's dues. That leaves time for the answers to change them. Keep it away from the week of your annual conference, and ask about the conference itself in a separate post event survey while attendees still remember the sessions.

faq_plan.q: Should a membership survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Not if staff need to follow up on what members say. A named survey lets staff call back after a low renewal score and split results by tier and join year. An anonymous one can draw franker comments on dues and staff, but no one can follow up on them. If you collect names, say so in the invitation and name who reads the comments.

faq_plan.q: Should a membership survey ask how likely members are to renew?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if the answer arrives while staff can still act on it. Ask at least a month before the renewal date, and follow any low score with an open question about what would change the member's mind. An app built with Emergent keeps each score next to the member's renewal date, in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How do I run a membership survey for members who do not use email?
faq_plan.a: Offer two other ways to answer. Staff can call the member and enter the answers into the same survey, or mail a printed copy and type in the returned answers. Record how each answer came in, then compare phone answers with online ones. A congregation with older members can do the same for its church survey.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Membership Survey That Shows Why Members Renew'; hero 'Build a membership survey that ties each answer to the member's tier and renewal date, with every response in your own database.'; how-to description 'Seven steps to create a membership survey members finish, then act on its answers before renewals come due.'

intent.evidence: Top 10 is question lists and templates for associations; the page gives questions (FAQ 1 'why the member joined, which benefits they used in the past year, and whether the dues feel fair'), template advice (FAQ 4), examples (FAQ 5 and four tabs: association, gym, makerspace, museum) and a 7-step how-to.

specificity.evidence: Member vocabulary: 'tier, join year, and renewal date', 'a student sees the ones on student dues', '351 took a CE course last year and 83 read the print journal', 'lapsed members'. Table from the library (QC V2/V3 pass).

openers.evidence: Full-sentence openers: 'Emergent writes questions for each member type you name', 'Upload your member list...', 'The Tamsworth Dental Hygienists' Association sends...', 'List the decisions this survey feeds'.

craft.evidence: QC Q2/Q5/Q7 clean; short single-idea sentences, e.g. 'The other 3 score 7 or higher and get no follow-up.'

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail: 'Merge duplicate records, fix emails that bounced, and leave lapsed members out of this send.' 'Keep the paper copies until the counts match the stack.'

truth.evidence: Claims map to approved ids: api-connect ('connect your membership software by API'), alerts ('emails the staff member... or posts in Slack'), conversational ('one question at a time'), code-export ('On paid plans'), database-owned, no-caps, ai-extraction ('sends any field it reads with low confidence to a person'). No statement of world fact needing a source. No anonymity claim: responses are tied to member records and the union answer promises only that management will not see answers. Numbers agree copy to image (434/1,240 = 35%, 351 = 81%, 83 = 19% and cover 19%; 2 of 5 at 6 or lower; 32+23+13 <= 85; 37/118 = 31%).

distinct.evidence: Own angle (renewal and benefit-use decisions); no sibling primary in a heading; church survey linked, not targeted.

The other 8 items are sourced and on topic; FAQ 10 'for a fan club' keeps its source's fan-club intent; no brand or file format in any question.

findings.quote: How do I do a membership survey for a union?
findings.issue: The recorded source is the Semrush question 'how do i do bts membership survey' (a K-pop fan-club membership). Swapping the brand for 'a union' changes the subject, so the item is a question no recorded searcher asked. HUB_RULES 5: FAQ items are sourced from what people actually search, never invented, light grammar edits only; DECISIONS ruling 12 treats a drifting question as blocking. FAQ 10 already covers the fan-club intent of the same keyword family.

findings.issue: Off-intent for a page about building membership surveys. The source keyword 'how to get bighit membership survey' is a fan trying to receive one club's survey (navigational/consumer intent), and the answer is consumer help ('Check the inbox of the email address you joined with, the spam folder included ... ask the club's support team'). It does not help anyone build a membership survey, and it fails the original searcher too, who wanted one specific club's survey. Same class as Divit's ruling 18 swaps of navigational and wrong-sense questions (address-verification-form Q10 navigational, vendor-application Q9 navigational, church-membership-form Q8 not the form). The answer's opening also states an unsourced generalisation about fan clubs ('a fan club sends its membership survey only to the members on its list'). Q10 already covers the fan-club organiser side.
